about: Lab design (the Experimental Design and Analysis trainer). Each experiment unlocks with the topic that teaches its physics; the first, the ramp, with motion-representations. Model: physics/assets/tools/math/lab-design.js; validator: scripts/lib/apphys-tool-checks/lab-design.mjs.
intro: Run an experiment on a lab bench: choose what to change, take real-looking measurements (each instrument has its own scatter), plot them, and find the graph that makes a straight line. The best-fit line's slope then gives a physical quantity: the cart's acceleration, g from a pendulum, a spring constant, the mass of a system, a pulley's rotational inertia or a liquid's density.
howItWorksTitle: How to design and analyze an experiment
howItWorks:
• Variables. The independent variable is the one you set; the dependent variable is the one you measure; everything else is held constant (the controls).
  • Instruments. Meterstick: a length. Stopwatch: a time (time many swings and divide). Motion detector: position over time, and from it velocity and acceleration. Spring scale or force sensor: a force. Balance: a mass. Photogate: when something passes a point.
  • Linearize. Write the model, then choose what to put on each axis so it reads y = (slope)·x + intercept. T = 2π√(L/g) becomes T² = (4π²/g)·L: graph T² against L.
  • Best-fit line. A straight line through the trend of the points (not dot to dot). Find the slope from two points on the line, far apart.
  • Use the slope. Match the slope to the symbols in the model (slope = 4π²/g, so g = 4π²/slope) and keep the units.
  • Error. An offset that is the same in every reading moves the line but not its slope. An error that grows with the reading (a percentage) changes the slope.

Data come from the physics with seeded noise sized to each instrument. g = 9.8 m/s². In the drill a slope counts within 6% of the least-squares slope, and the quantity from it within 6%.
